lessons.title: Milking Techniques and Hygiene
lessons.body: Milking a goat properly takes about 5 minutes per goat once you are skilled. Wash your hands with soap and clean water before touching the udder. Use a stainless steel bucket, not plastic, because plastic scratches hide bacteria. Clean the udder with a warm damp cloth, then dry with a clean towel. Discard the first few squirts of milk into a separate cup because they contain the most bacteria. Squeeze the teat gently but firmly between thumb and forefinger, then roll your fingers down to push milk out. Do not pull or yank. Use a full-hand grip, not just two fingers. Keep a calm environment; goats milk best when relaxed. In Africa, many farmers milk twice a day: early morning and late afternoon. Leave the kid with the mother at night if you milk in the morning, or separate them for 12 hours before milking. Always milk at the same times daily. After milking, dip teats in a teat dip solution (iodine-based) to prevent mastitis. Strain the milk through a clean cloth or filter into a clean container. Wash all equipment with hot water and dish soap, then rinse with clean water and air dry upside down. Never use the same cloth for cleaning udders and equipment. Keep records: date, goat ID, amount of milk. A good dairy goat gives 2-3 litres per day. If milk is bloody or lumpy, that goat has mastitis; treat it and do not sell that milk.

lessons.title: Milk Handling and Storage
lessons.body: Fresh goat milk spoils within 2 hours in African heat if not cooled. After straining, put milk in a clean glass or food-grade plastic container with a tight lid. Cool it immediately by placing the container in a bucket of cold water, or in a fridge if you have one. If no fridge, use a clay pot (zeer) or a wet sack: put the milk container inside a larger pot, fill the gap with wet sand, and keep it in the shade. Change the wet sand every few hours. This can keep milk cool for up to 12 hours. Never store milk in metal containers like aluminium pots because they give a metallic taste. Keep milk away from strong smells like onions, diesel, or soap. Use within 48 hours if refrigerated, or within 8 hours if only cooled with wet sand. For longer storage, boil the milk: heat to 85Â°C (just before boiling), hold for 15 seconds, then cool quickly. This pasteurisation kills most bacteria and gives 5-7 days in a fridge. If you sell raw milk, label it clearly and tell customers to boil before drinking. Always use clean containers: wash with hot water and soap, then rinse with boiling water. Never mix morning and evening milk unless both are cooled to the same temperature. Test milk before selling: smell it (should be fresh, slightly sweet), look at it (no lumps), and taste a drop (not sour). If it smells sour or looks stringy, discard it.

lessons.title: Milk Processing: Cheese and Yogurt
lessons.body: To make yogurt: heat 1 litre of goat milk to 85Â°C, then cool to 45Â°C (you can test with a clean finger â it should feel warm but not hot). Add 2 tablespoons of plain yogurt with live cultures as a starter. Stir well, cover, and keep warm (around 40-45Â°C) for 6-8 hours. In Africa, wrap the pot in a blanket or put it in a thermos. When it thickens, refrigerate. For cheese: heat 4 litres of milk to 32Â°C. Add 1/2 teaspoon of rennet diluted in 1/4 cup of cool water. Stir gently for 30 seconds, then leave for 45 minutes until curds form. Cut curds into 1 cm cubes, then heat slowly to 40Â°C while stirring. Drain whey through a cheesecloth. For a simple fresh cheese (like chÃ¨vre), hang the curds in cloth for 6 hours, then add salt and herbs. Press for a firmer cheese. Yield: 4 litres of milk gives about 500g of fresh cheese. Always use clean pots and utensils. For a soft cheese, you can also add lemon juice (1/4 cup per litre) to hot milk to curdle it. That gives paneer-style cheese. Store cheese in a fridge or cool place for up to 2 weeks. Yogurt lasts 1-2 weeks refrigerated. Sell in clean jars with lids. Label with date and type.

lessons.title: Dairy Goat Management
lessons.body: Dairy goats need better feed than meat goats. A milking doe needs 16-18% protein in her diet. Give her 1 kg of dairy meal (commercial or homemade: maize bran, cottonseed cake, and minerals) per 2 litres of milk produced. Also provide free-choice hay or fresh legume fodder like lucerne, desmodium, or sweet potato vines. Clean water at all times: a milking doe drinks 10-15 litres daily. Without water, milk drops fast. Minerals are critical: provide a salt lick with copper and selenium. In Africa, copper deficiency is common in goats, causing poor milk and health. Keep goats in a clean, dry house with 1.5 square metres per adult goat. Dirty bedding causes mastitis and foot rot. Trim hooves every 3 months. Vaccinate against CCPP and enterotoxaemia. Deworm every 3-6 months depending on load. Breed dairy goats like Toggenburg, Saanen, or their crosses with local goats for adaptability. A good doe produces 2-4 litres per day for 10 months after kidding. To keep milk flowing, milk twice daily at 12-hour intervals. Dry off the doe 2 months before next kidding. Keep records of milk per goat per day. Cull does that give less than 1 litre per day after their second kidding. Provide shade and ventilation; heat stress reduces milk by up to 30%.

lessons.title: Milk Quality Testing
lessons.body: You can test milk quality without a lab. First, the alcohol test: mix equal parts milk and 68% ethanol (or strong local gin) in a clean bottle. If curds form, the milk is acidic or has mastitis â reject it. Second, the clot-on-boiling test: boil a small sample. If it curdles, it is not fresh. Third, the lactometer test: use a lactometer to check density. Pure goat milk reads 1.026-1.034 at 20Â°C. If lower, it may be watered down. Fourth, the sediment test: filter 500 ml through a white cloth. Dirt or manure means poor hygiene. Fifth, smell and taste: fresh goat milk has a slightly sweet taste and no strong smell. Sour smell means bacteria. For mastitis, use the California Mastitis Test (CMT): mix milk with CMT reagent, look for gel formation. Or simply strip milk onto a dark surface â lumps, blood, or watery milk indicate mastitis. Always test before selling or processing. Keep a thermometer to check milk temperature: should be below 4Â°C for cold chain. If you sell to a dairy, they will test with these methods. Train your workers to do the alcohol test daily. Record results per goat. If a goat fails, treat and do not mix her milk with the bulk tank.

lessons.title: Marketing Dairy Products
lessons.body: Sell milk, yogurt, and cheese where people already buy food: local markets, schools, hospitals, and restaurants. In many African cities, fresh goat milk sells for 2-3 times the price of cow milk because it is easier to digest and good for children and the elderly. Target health-conscious customers and those with cow milk allergies. Package milk in 500 ml or 1 litre clean bottles with a label showing your farm name, date, and 'keep refrigerated'. For yogurt, use 250 ml or 500 ml jars. Sell plain and flavoured (vanilla, strawberry). Cheese: sell fresh chÃ¨vre in 200g rounds wrapped in paper or vacuum bags. Price your products: calculate cost of feed, labour, packaging, and transport, then add 30-50% profit. For example, if 1 litre of milk costs 50 KES to produce, sell at 80-100 KES. For yogurt, 1 litre of milk makes 1 litre of yogurt; sell at 150-200 KES. Build a brand: give free samples at markets. Use WhatsApp groups and Facebook Marketplace to take orders. Partner with local shops that take a 10-15% commission. Deliver on time and keep products cold. Always keep records of sales and expenses. Reinvest profits into better feed and more goats. As you grow, consider selling to supermarkets or hotels â they need consistent supply and quality. Never sell spoiled products; it destroys trust.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Dairy Goat Milk Production in Africa

Dairy goats deliver one of the fastest returns on investment in African smallholder livestock. A single improved doe â Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine, or their crosses with local East African and West African Dwarf goats â can produce 2â4 litres of milk per day across a 250â300 day lactation. At prevailing farmgate prices of USD 0.60â1.20 per litre in Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda, and Nigeria, that is USD 450â1,400 of gross milk income per doe per year, before you count manure, meat, or breeding stock. This Practical Reference brings together the operational numbers, hygiene standards, and processing options you need to run a profitable dairy goat enterprise.

1. Milking Techniques and Hygiene

Milk is 87% water and an ideal bacterial growth medium. Every 10 minutes of delay at ambient temperature in the tropics doubles the bacterial load. The commercial consequence is simple: buyers reject high-bacterial milk, processors pay less, and shelf life collapses from 3 days to under 12 hours.

Milking routine for a 2â4 litre doe takes 4â6 minutes by hand. Use a clean, dry, quiet pen. Wash hands and udder with potable water (chlorinated at 200 ppm if from a borehole), dry with a clean cloth used for that doe alone, and strip the first 2â3 squirts into a black-bottomed strip cup to check for clots, blood, or watery milk â the first sign of mastitis. Milk with a full-hand squeeze, not thumb-and-finger pinching, which damages teat tissue. After milking, dip teats in iodine or chlorhexidine solution. Feed the doe immediately after milking so she remains standing and the teat canal closes before she lies down.

Milk twice daily at 12-hour intervals. Once-daily milking is possible for low-yielding local does but reduces yield by 20â30% in improved breeds. Always milk kids-first in the first 3 days to ensure colostrum intake, then switch to twice-daily for the doe.

2. Milk Handling and Storage

The single most important rule: cool milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours of milking and keep it there. In off-grid African conditions, use a chest freezer with frozen water bottles, a charcoal evaporative cooler (zeer pot), or a solar-powered milk chiller. Stainless steel or food-grade aluminium cans are the standard; plastic jerrycans are the leading cause of high bacterial counts and off-flavours on smallholder farms.

Table 1: Milk storage life by temperature (goat milk, raw)
Storage temperatureSafe storage lifeBacterial growthPractical method in rural Africa

15â20Â°C8â10 hoursModerateShaded, ventilated room, wet cloth wrap
4â8Â°C48â72 hoursSlowFridge, solar chiller, evaporative cooler

Source: FAO/WHO Code of Hygienic Practice for Milk and Milk Products (CAC/RCP 57-2004); ILRI Milk Handling Guidelines for Smallholders (2018).

3. Milk Processing: Cheese and Yogurt

Processing roughly doubles the value of a litre of milk. A litre that sells raw for USD 0.80 becomes 1.2 kg of fresh cheese worth USD 3.00â4.00, or 1 litre of yogurt retailing at USD 1.50â2.00. Start with yogurt â lower capital, faster turnover, and a ready market in urban and peri-urban areas. Cheese follows once you have consistent cold-chain and a buyer.

Yogurt: Pasteurise milk at 85Â°C for 15 minutes (kills pathogens and denatures whey proteins for a firmer set), cool to 43Â°C, inoculate with 2% active culture (or 100 ml of previous batch per 5 L), incubate at 42â45Â°C for 4â6 hours until set, then chill to 4Â°C. Flavour with sugar, fruit, or vanilla. Package in 250 ml or 500 ml cups with a foil seal. Shelf life: 14â21 days refrigerated.

Fresh cheese (chÃ¨vre-style): Pasteurise, cool to 22Â°C, add rennet (1 ml per 10 L) and mesophilic culture, let set 12â18 hours, cut the curd, drain in muslin for 12â24 hours, salt at 1â1.5%, and pack. Yield: 1 L milk â 200â250 g fresh cheese. Shelf life: 7â14 days chilled.

â  SAFETY WARNING â RAW MILK AND BRUCELLOSIS

Goats carry Brucella melitensis, Mycobacterium bovis, and E. coli O157:H7. Raw goat milk is a documented transmission route for brucellosis (Malta fever), which causes undulant fever in humans and can become chronic. In many African countries raw milk sale is restricted or banned for retail.

  • Always pasteurise milk for yogurt, cheese, and any product sold to the public (63Â°C for 30 min, or 72Â°C for 15 sec).
  • Test your herd annually for brucellosis; cull positive animals. Never drink milk from an untested doe.
  • Wear gloves when handling aborting does â Brucella is shed in placenta and uterine fluids.
  • If you or a worker develop recurring fever after handling raw milk, seek medical testing for brucellosis immediately.

4. Dairy Goat Management

A dairy doe needs 16â18% crude protein concentrate plus good-quality forage (Napier grass, lucerne, sweet potato vines, or tree fodder such as Leucaena and Calliandra) to produce 3 litres/day. Feed 0.4 kg concentrate per litre of milk above 1 litre maintenance. Provide clean water ad libitum â a milking doe drinks 8â12 litres/day. Minerals (especially calcium and selenium) and a salt lick prevent milk fever and white muscle disease.

Breeding: aim for a 12-month kidding interval. Wean kids at 3 months, rebreed the doe 60â90 days after kidding, and dry her off 60 days before the next kidding. Keep records of milk yield, kidding dates, and health treatments â this is what turns a goat herd into a business.

Table 2: Performance benchmarks and economics â dairy goats in East Africa

Sources: ILRI Dairy Goat Production in East Africa (2019); FAO Small-Scale Dairy Farming Manual (2011); KALRO Dairy Goat Enterprise Budget (2020); SNV East Africa Dairy Market Assessment (2021).

5. Milk Quality Testing

Three field tests every smallholder can run:

  • Alcohol test (68% ethanol): Mix equal parts milk and alcohol. If it clots, the milk is acidic â reject or process immediately into cheese. Cost: under USD 5 for a year's supply.
  • Clot-on-boiling test: Boil 5 ml of milk. If it curdles, the milk is already sour and unsuitable for sale or yogurt.
  • Lactometer / density test: Goat milk should read 1.026â1.034 at 20Â°C. Low readings indicate added water; high readings may indicate added solids or mastitis milk.

For a co-op or processor, add a somatic cell count (SCC) test â healthy goat milk is below 1,000,000 cells/ml, and premium milk is below 500,000. Also test for antibiotic residues if you treat does; withdrawal periods are 3â5 days for most intramammary antibiotics.

6. Marketing Dairy Products

Your market determines your processing. Three realistic channels in Africa:

  • Neighbourhood / direct retail: Highest price per litre (USD 0.80â1.20), no cold chain needed if sold within hours. Best for raw milk where legal, and for yogurt in urban estates.
  • Co-operative / processor: Lower price (USD 0.40â0.70) but guaranteed volume and payment. Requires consistent quality and daily delivery. Examples: Brookside (Kenya), Lamex (Ethiopia), Pearl Dairy (Uganda).
  • Value-added / branded: Yogurt, cheese, and flavoured milk sold under your own label to hotels, supermarkets, and schools. Highest margin (USD 1.50â4.00 per litre equivalent), but requires packaging, cold chain, and food-safety compliance.

Price your product against the local alternative, not against your cost. A 500 ml yogurt cup that replaces a USD 1.20 imported brand can sell for USD 0.90 and still return 3Ã the raw milk price. Build a brand around freshness, hygiene, and local sourcing â these are the three things African consumers pay a premium for.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Milk twice daily at 12-hour intervals; wash and dry udder with a doe-specific cloth.
  2. Discard foremilk into a strip cup and check for mastitis before every milking.
  3. Cool milk to 4Â°C within 2 hours; never store in plastic jerrycans.
  4. Pasteurise all milk for yogurt, cheese, and any public sale.
  5. Test annually for brucellosis; cull positive animals; wear gloves for abortions.
  6. Feed 0.4 kg concentrate per litre of milk above maintenance, plus minerals and water.
  7. Run the alcohol and clot-on-boiling tests before every sale or processing batch.
  8. Keep records of yield, kidding, health, and input costs â review monthly.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-Scale Dairy Farming Manual (free, full text)
  • ILRI â Dairy Goat Production in East Africa and related publications
  • FAO â Milk and Dairy Products in Human Nutrition
  • Codex Alimentarius â Code of Hygienic Practice for Milk and Milk Products (CAC/RCP 57-2004)
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (dairy goat enterprise resources)

quiz.q: What should you do with the first few squirts of milk during milking?
options: A) Add them to the main bucket
C) Give them to the kid
quiz.explanation: The first squirts contain the highest bacterial load and should be discarded to improve milk quality.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a milking bucket?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel is easy to clean and does not scratch, reducing bacterial hiding places.

quiz.q: How often should you milk a dairy goat for good production?
quiz.explanation: Twice daily at 12-hour intervals maintains milk production and udder health.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of teat dipping after milking?
quiz.explanation: Teat dipping with iodine-based solution kills bacteria that cause mastitis.

quiz.q: How long can fresh goat milk last if cooled with wet sand in a clay pot?
quiz.explanation: Wet sand cooling can keep milk cool for up to 12 hours if kept in shade and sand kept wet.

quiz.q: Which container should you avoid for storing milk?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium gives a metallic taste and can react with milk acids.

quiz.q: What temperature should milk be heated to for pasteurisation?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 85Â°C for 15 seconds kills most bacteria without boiling.

quiz.q: What should you do if milk smells sour?
quiz.explanation: Sour smell indicates spoilage; consuming or selling it is unsafe.

quiz.q: How much starter yogurt is needed for 1 litre of milk to make yogurt?
quiz.explanation: 2 tablespoons of live yogurt provides enough culture to ferment 1 litre.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for adding rennet to milk for cheese?
quiz.explanation: Rennet works best at around 32Â°C for proper curd formation.

quiz.q: How much fresh cheese can you get from 4 litres of goat milk?
quiz.explanation: Yield is about 500g of fresh cheese from 4 litres of milk.

quiz.q: Which acid can be used to curdle milk for paneer-style cheese?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice (1/4 cup per litre) curdles hot milk to make paneer.

quiz.q: How much protein should a milking doe's diet contain?
quiz.explanation: Dairy goats need 16-18% protein for optimal milk production.

quiz.q: How much water does a milking doe need daily?
quiz.explanation: A milking doe drinks 10-15 litres of water daily to support milk production.

quiz.q: What mineral deficiency is common in African goats and affects milk?
quiz.explanation: Copper deficiency is common and leads to poor milk and health problems.

quiz.q: How often should you trim hooves of dairy goats?
quiz.explanation: Trimming every 3 months prevents foot problems and maintains mobility.

quiz.q: What is the alcohol test used for in milk quality?
options: B) To detect acidity or mastitis
quiz.explanation: Alcohol test causes curdling if milk is acidic or from a mastitis-infected goat.

quiz.q: What does a lactometer reading of 1.026-1.034 indicate?
quiz.explanation: This density range is normal for pure goat milk at 20Â°C.

quiz.q: What should you do if milk fails the alcohol test?
options: C) Reject and treat the goat
quiz.explanation: Failing indicates poor quality or mastitis; reject the milk and treat the goat.

quiz.q: What is the California Mastitis Test (CMT) used for?
quiz.explanation: CMT reagent forms a gel with milk from a mastitis-infected udder.

quiz.q: Why is goat milk often sold at a higher price than cow milk in African cities?
options: A) It is harder to produce
B) It is easier to digest and good for allergies
quiz.explanation: Goat milk is easier to digest and suitable for those with cow milk allergies.

quiz.q: What packaging size is suggested for selling fresh goat milk?
quiz.explanation: 500 ml and 1 litre bottles are convenient for customers.

quiz.q: How much profit margin is recommended when pricing dairy products?
quiz.explanation: Adding 30-50% profit covers costs and allows reinvestment.

quiz.q: What is a good way to promote dairy products locally?
options: B) Give free samples at markets
C) Wait for customers to come
quiz.explanation: Free samples let people taste the quality and encourage purchases.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have no fridge for milk storage?
options: A) Keep it in the sun
B) Use a clay pot with wet sand
quiz.explanation: A clay pot with wet sand acts as an evaporative cooler to keep milk cool.

quiz.q: How long can pasteurised milk last in a fridge?
quiz.explanation: Pasteurisation at 85Â°C for 15 seconds gives 5-7 days refrigerated shelf life.

quiz.q: What is the first step before milking a goat?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands prevents bacteria from contaminating the milk.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of mastitis in milk?
quiz.explanation: Lumps, blood, or watery milk indicate mastitis infection.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space per adult goat in a dairy house?
quiz.explanation: 1.5 square metres per adult goat reduces stress and disease.

quiz.q: What is the best way to cool milk immediately after milking if you have a fridge?
options: A) Put it in the freezer
B) Place in cold water then fridge
quiz.explanation: Cooling in cold water first then refrigerating brings temperature down quickly and safely.
